summary: Travis Kelce said on his podcast New Heights that the NFL is "overdoing it a little bit" with its Taylor Swift coverage during the 1 October Chiefs-Jets game, agreeing with his brother Jason, who titled the episode "The NFL Needs to Calm Down". The coverage still boosted ratings and Kelce's jersey sales, and the brothers also talked about their mother Donna Kelce enjoying the star-studded suite. The NFL responded with a statement to People saying it leaned into a pop cultural moment while most content stayed focused on the game.
one_line: Travis Kelce agrees on his podcast that the NFL is overdoing its Taylor Swift coverage, even as ratings and jersey sales surge.
key_facts: Travis Kelce, 33, is a Kansas City Chiefs tight end who discussed the NFL's coverage on his podcast New Heights with Jason and Travis Kelce after the 1 October game against the New York Jets.
The game was played at MetLife Stadium, and fans complained about constant Taylor Swift references during the broadcast.
Swift's suite guests included Blake Lively, Ryan Reynolds, Sophie Turner and Hugh Jackman.
The NFL ran a special segment with Carson Daly and The Voice to explain football to "Swifties".
The podcast episode was titled "The NFL Needs to Calm Down"; Jason Kelce, 35, a Philadelphia Eagles player, said "They're overdoing it" and Travis agreed "a little bit, for sure".
Travis Kelce said the coverage "brings a little more to the atmosphere" and that the NFL is "just trying to have fun with it".
Per a Deadline report, NBC averaged 27m viewers, with 29m tuning in during the second quarter; Jason Kelce called it a likely NFL record.
About two million viewers were estimated to be female, according to Jason Kelce's remarks on the podcast.
Donna Kelce, known as "Mama Kelce", travelled from Philadelphia to New Jersey to watch both her sons play on 1 October.
Travis Kelce said his mom was "sitting there with Deadpool and Wolverine", referring to Reynolds and Jackman's superhero roles.
Chiefs tight end jersey sales have reportedly spiked 400 per cent, according to the NFL's e-commerce partner Fanatics.
In a statement to People on 4 October, the NFL said the Swift and Kelce news was "a pop cultural moment we've leaned into in real time" and that most content stayed focused on the game.
